abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

title: The advances and challenges of mRNA-LNP application in fields of hematology and oncology therapeutics.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed RNA therapeutics through their high delivery efficiency, scalable manufacturing, and favorable safety profiles, as demonstrated by COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and clinically approved small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics. However, extending RNA delivery beyond the liver to extrahepatic tissues, including the spleen, lungs, lymph nodes, brain, and tumors, remains challenging because of the intrinsic hepatotropism of conventional LNPs and their limited cell-type specificity. Recent advances in lipid chemistry, particle engineering, surface functionalization, protein corona modulation, and route-specific administration have enabled new strategies to redirect LNPs toward specific tissues and cell populations. This review systematically examines these approaches and highlights key determinants of LNP tropism, including formulation composition, surface properties, endogenous protein adsorption, and administration route. We further discuss the clinical translation of extrahepatic LNP delivery, covering clinically validated products, emerging therapeutic candidates, and gaps between preclinical models and human applications. Major challenges include cell-resolved biodistribution, long-term safety, repeated-dose immunogenicity, cross-study comparability, and standardized quantitative assessment. Finally, we explore how high-throughput screening, machine learning, and data-driven design can accelerate the rational optimization of next-generation LNPs. These advances may facilitate precise tissue- and cell-selective RNA delivery, expanding the therapeutic potential of RNA medicines beyond the liver.

abstract: Introduction In February 2025, a single infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency received a customized base-editing therapy, and individualized gene editing has since been discussed as an emerging category of care. No one has yet counted whether this category exists in the registered study record. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional census of interventional studies of human gene-editing agents registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Records were retrieved through the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface, version 2, with a verbatim, intervention-scoped query and a fixed census date of 17 September 2026. Eligibility was verified from each record's own fields, and every exclusion is supported by the field value that justifies it. Two independent screening passes classified each eligible record as single-participant or n-of-1, multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated, or conventional cohort. Agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Records in the individualized and platform classes were re-verified against their complete registry entries and version histories. We also searched public US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) records for the regulatory route of each census record. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. Results Of 212 retrieved records, 64 were excluded, and 148 were eligible. Four eligible records were single-participant or n-of-1 designs, and three were multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated designs, giving a census of seven studies. Of the remainder, 140 were conventional cohorts, and one was an editing arm inside a non-editing platform trial. Version histories confirmed the four single-participant designs; one of them reached an enrolment of one through a revision made before enrolment began. The same histories showed that three other records had an enrolment of one or two only because of termination or under-enrolment. Only two of the 148 eligible records describe a construct designed for the individual participant. No publicly verifiable platform technology designation was located for any census record, and the census query returned no expanded-access record. Of 23 studies completed more than 12 months before the census, five had posted results (21.7%, Wilson 95% CI: 9.7%-41.9%); because this interval is wide, the figure is reported as context only. Agreement on design class was moderate (kappa, 0.540; 95% CI, 0.264-0.815). Conclusions Nineteen months after the first individualized CRISPR treatment, the registry contains seven individualized or platform-designated gene-editing studies, and only two records describe an individualized construct. The regulatory pathway used by the index case was not retrievable from the registry, and no regulatory route could be verified from public records; this is an absence of public evidence, not evidence that no route existed. These counts describe the ClinicalTrials.gov record, not the prevalence of individualized gene editing, and the design-class counts are provisional given moderate agreement.

abstract: Infant neuroblastoma (NB), defined by diagnosis during the first year of life, represents a clinically heterogeneous disease spectrum ranging from localized tumours with favourable outcomes and a capacity for spontaneous regression, to high-risk metastatic disease requiring intensive multimodal therapy. In infants, treatment intensity is determined by disease stage, tumor biology, MYCN status, risk classification, symptoms, response to therapy, and metastatic involvement, particularly relevant to high-risk disease, consequently the potential toxicity of intensive treatment is specific to high-risk disease, as compared to favorable risk tumors which can be managed with surgery, reduced frequency techniques, or observations. Important determinations of neuroblastoma biology and prognosis are genetic alterations involving MYCN and ALK, but the predominately investigated field with therapeutic feasibility of targeting these changes with CRISPR/Cas9 is in preclinical neuroblastoma models rather than in infants. An investigational hypothesis is accordingly considered by their potential relevance to infant neuroblastoma rather than an established clinical application. The safe and efficient in vivo delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 components remains a major challenge, owing to cargo size, immunogenicity, and degradation, particularly within the delicate physiological environment of infants. This review emphasises the need for advanced delivery systems, focusing on the potential of nanoparticle-mediated approaches. Emerging preclinical findings support the feasibility of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 delivery, although direct evidence in infant neuroblastoma remains limited. Importantly, the evidence for nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 therapy remains largely preclinical. Studies performed in general neuroblastoma models, non-cancer models, or adult cancers should not be interpreted as direct evidence of efficacy in infant neuroblastoma.

title: Precision gene editing in infant neuroblastoma: a review of nanoparticle: enabled CRISPR/Cas9 therapies.

abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers in cancer: emerging platforms for molecular imaging, biosensing, and precision oncology.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations.
RESULTS: We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79,648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing.
AVAILABILITY: CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a pivotal regulator of cholesterol homeostasis, primarily known for inducing the degradation of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). Beyond this classical pathway, PCSK9 exerts complex pleiotropic effects and interacts with various lipoproteins, contributing to cardiovascular and metabolic pathologies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on PCSK9 biology, its multi-organ implications and evolving therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes current evidence from experimental, translational and clinical studies on PCSK9 biology and therapeutics. The literature examined includes studies on PCSK9 transcriptional regulation, post-translational modifications, interactions with lipoproteins and the clinical development of established and emerging PCSK9-targeting therapies.
RESULTS: PCSK9 activity is modulated by several transcription factors (e.g., SREBP2, HNF1α) and post-translational processes such as furin cleavage and sulfation. Clinically, elevated PCSK9 levels are linked to atherosclerosis progression, heart failure and adverse outcomes in infectious diseases and certain malignancies. Monoclonal antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab) and siRNA (inclisiran) consistently reduce LDL-C by 50%-60%. Emerging approaches include oral inhibitors which may broaden access to PCSK9-targeting therapy, and CRISPR-based gene-editing strategies (e.g., VERVE-102), which aim to achieve sustained LDL-C lowering after a single treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: PCSK9 is a multifaceted protein with roles extending far beyond LDL-C regulation. Understanding its diverse interactions is crucial for optimizing treatment in cardiovascular disease and potentially expanding its therapeutic application to metabolic and infectious conditions.

title: Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9: From Biology to Therapeutic Targeting in Cardiovascular Disease.

abstract:
AIMS: Selenoprotein T (SELENOT) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident thioredoxin-like oxidoreductase implicated in redox and calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis and protein quality control. Although SELENOT is highly expressed in the brain, its role in hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons, which regulate energy balance, remains poorly understood. We investigated whether SELENOT is required for maintaining ER homeostasis and neuronal integrity in POMC neurons.
RESULTS: Using CRISPR-edited and siRNA-silenced POMC neuronal models together with a POMC-specific SELENOT knockout mouse, we demonstrated that SELENOT loss induces a senescent-like phenotype including cellular hypertrophy, loss of neurite outgrowth, senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, increased P16 and P21 expression, and acquisition of senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Senescence markers were elevated not only in SELENOT-deficient POMC neurons but also throughout the surrounding arcuate nucleus in vivo, suggesting propagation of a pro-inflammatory microenvironment. Mechanistically, prolonged SELENOT deficiency produced selective activation of the ATF6α arm of the unfolded protein response, depletion of ER Ca2+ stores, and profound alterations in N-glycan maturation. Notably, leptin-induced POMC processing and secretion were spared. Glycomics revealed a shift toward immature glycans, whereas thiol-trapping proteomics identified candidate SELENOT interactors linked to ER Ca2+ regulation.
INNOVATION AND CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first evidence that SELENOT deficiency is sufficient to trigger cellular senescence in POMC neurons, acting as a central regulator integrating ER proteostasis, Ca2+ homeostasis, redox adaptation, and glycosylation. These results reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism potentially linking neuronal senescence to hypothalamic dysfunction and suggest that SELENOT-dependent pathways may represent therapeutic targets for obesity, metabolic disease, and age-related neuroendocrine disorders. abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.

abstract: This is an open-label, dose escalation study in patients with relapsed and refractory autoimmune diseases. Study drug, TI-0032-III injection, is composed of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) targeting T cells that encapsulate circular RNA encoding the CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), which is a therapeutic biological product. It is clinically intended for the treatment of various relapsed and refractory B cell-related autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, and antiphospholipid syndrome.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

abstract:
Background:

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis syndrome (WHIMs) is a rare disorder that affects the immune system. People with WHIMs can have severe infections all over their body. WHIMs is caused by a mutation in the CXCR4 gene. Treatment with drugs can help control the infections but does not cure the disorder. Researchers want to try a treatment where they collect stem cells from a person with WHIMS, use base-editing to replace the bad gene with a healthy version, and return the new cells to the person. This could cure WHIMs.

Objective:

To test a treatment using base-edited stem cells in people with WHIMs.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with WHIMs.

Design:

The study has 4 stages.

Stage 1: Screening. Participants will be screened at 1 or more visits. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. A sample of tissue and fluid (biopsy) will be taken from the bone marrow in the hip.

Stage 2: Apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle; the blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Stage 3: Treatment. Participants will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks. They will receive 3 drugs to prepare their body for the procedure. Then the edited stem cells will be returned to their bloodstream. They will stay in the hospital until they recover.

Stage 4: Follow-up. Participants will have 8 follow-up visits over 5 years. Long-term visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) base-edited to repair CXCR4 mutations in 10 participants with (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, and Myelokathexis) WHIM syndrome.

Primary Objective: Evaluate safety of treatment with BE-HSPC CXCR4 in participants with WHIM syndrome.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate:

* Efficacy.
* Genetic correction.
* Immune reconstitution.
* Clinical efficacy.

Exploratory Objective:

Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety assessed by:

* Incidence of adverse events (AEs) for each participant.
* Evaluate overall incidence of AEs for the study.
* Incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs).

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

* Efficacy: \>= 5% gene edited circulating myeloid cells by 12 months after BE HSPC infusion.
* Gene correction:

  --Frequency of corrected alleles in peripheral blood cells (such as myeloid, T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).

  --\>200/microL edited neutrophils by 12 months post receipt of the BE HSPC infusion.
* Immune reconstitution:

  * T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
  * B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
* Clinical efficacy: Improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, wart burden, gastrointestinal complaints, or immune dysregulation.

Exploratory Endpoint:

Evaluate for frequency of OTs by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at the genomic locus 2 years post-infusion.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.

trial.official_title: A Phase 3 Study of Dinutuximab Added to Intensive Multimodal Therapy for Children With Newly Diagnosed High-Risk Neuroblastoma

outcomes.description: EFS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B to first episode of disease relapse or progression, second malignancy, or death, or until last contact if no event has occurred.
outcomes.measure: Event free survival (EFS)

outcomes.description: The response rate will be calculated among all evaluable patients at end of Induction. Responders are defined as patients who achieve a \>= partial response per the revised 2017 International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC)
outcomes.measure: End of Induction (EOI) response rate
outcomes.time_frame: From randomization to end of extended Induction, up to 12 months

outcomes.description: OS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B until death, or until last contact if patient is alive.
outcomes.measure: Overall survival (OS)

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients with at least one grade 3 or higher non-hematologic toxicity or grade 4 or higher hematologic toxicity during protocol therapy, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, will be reported.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of adverse events

outcomes.description: Dinutuximab binding to pre-therapy patient tumor samples will be measured and categorized as high or low.
outcomes.measure: GD2 expression

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in Arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between tumor and host factors (including tumor ALK and other somatic mutations, copy-number aberrations, gene fusions, gene expression, and pathogenic germline variants) and chemo-immunotherapy during Induction with outcome.
outcomes.measure: Association between tumor and host factors and outcomes

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by comparing the proportion of patients with detectable vs. non-detectable tumor markers (including circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid, circulating free DNA, circulating tumor cells, and immune function profiling) between Arms A and B during and after induction and post-consolidation therapy using chi-squared tests at each individual time point, and Cochran's Q across time points to determine if there is a consistent difference in proportions between arms across time. In addition, the tumor markers will be analyzed as continuous variables using longitudinal data analysis methodology such as mixed effects models or generalized estimating equations as appropriate.
outcomes.measure: Circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease

outcomes.description: The impact of early or late chemoimmunotherapy during Induction on the probability of the involvement of a specific disease site at first relapse will be evaluated using Fisher's exact test.
outcomes.measure: Patterns of failure

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between telomere maintenance mechanism and chemoimmunotherapy during Induction with outcome. Patients will be classified into 3 groups by telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM) based on messenger ribonucleic acid expression of TERT and analysis of telomeric DNA C-circles: telomerase (TERT) positive, alternative of lengthening of telomeres (ALT) positive, or no identified TMM.
outcomes.measure: Effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms

outcomes.description: Will descriptively summarize and compare the total Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale scores, total sub-domain scores, and individual symptom scores between patients randomized to receive dinutuximab during Induction (Arm B) to those of patients randomized to standard Induction (Arm A).
outcomes.measure: Functional and quality of life outcomes
outcomes.time_frame: At serial time points during Induction, Extended Induction, Post-Consolidation, and at the end of therapy

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by descriptively comparing the successful delineation of histologic classification, MYCN amplification status, and ALK status via the traditional method of obtaining tissue for diagnosis, open surgical biopsy, versus the less invasive percutaneous core needle biopsy.
outcomes.measure: Adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens

outcomes.description: Kaplan-Meier curves of EFS and OS will be generated and used to calculate 3-year EFS and OS estimates. Associations between social determinants of health (SDOH) and survival outcomes and time to receipt of dinutuximab will be evaluated with univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard models. Log-binomial regression will be used to estimate risk ratios and 95% CI for the occurrence of dinutuximab consent to randomization and therapy receipt by SDOH exposure. Effect modification of outcomes as a function of poverty, stratified by race/ethnicity, will be explored.
outcomes.measure: Associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology

outcomes.description: Scans will be given as input to a convolutional neural network trained to predict EOI response.
outcomes.measure: Develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response (imaging objective)
outcomes.time_frame: At diagnosis, EOI, during Extended Induction, and end of Extended Induction

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by calculating the percentage of patients receiving the same EOI institutional and centrally reviewed determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and PEIR and GEIR. In addition, Cohen's kappa will be calculated to evaluate the concordance in each of these response measures.
outcomes.measure: Compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components, and PEIR and GEIR determination (imaging objective)

outcomes.description: Will be addressed by calculating the proportion of treated patients with each late effect, including but not limited to impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and secondary malignancy. A 95% confidence interval will be placed on each proportion.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of late toxicities

outcomes.description: The cumulative incidence of local progression (CILP) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI and GEIR on this study will be compared to the CILP rate of 11.2±1.8% observed on ANBL0532 using Gray's test.
outcomes.measure: Reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by calculating the incidence of endothelial injury complications and non-relapse mortality within 100 days of transplant, transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA), severe TA-TMA, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) on Arms A and B and comparing between arms with a chi-squared test. The impact of TA-TMA occurrence on the timing or exclusion of subsequent therapy and interventions utilized to treat the TA-TMA, and associations with outcomes (EFS and OS) will be assessed.
outcomes.measure: Post-transplant complications

outcomes.description: Log-rank tests will be used to explore the association between EOI response (using both the revised INRC and GEIR/PEIR classification) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).
outcomes.measure: Associations between end of induction (EOI) response and individual response components

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients in the analytic cohort for whom each particular IDRF and also the presence of any IDRF is absent prior to surgical resection will be computed. McNemar's test for paired observations will be applied to determine whether there is a difference in the proportion of each IDRF and any IDRF present before and after initial therapy, and conditional logistic regression will be used to compare between treatment arms A and B. The IDRF status after initial therapy and whether there has been a change from diagnosis will be associated with surgical outcome (complete vs. incomplete resection, presence or absence of surgical complications) using chi-squared tests, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The association of IDRF status with presence or absence of local failure after primary tumor resection will also be evaluated using a chi-squared test, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel.
outcomes.measure: Changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRF)

abstract: Trypanosoma brucei and Leishmania tarentolae are model kinetoplastids whose mitochondria contain a unique DNA network, kinetoplast DNA (kDNA), and exhibit specialized features, including developmental remodeling and RNA editing. By integrating mass spectrometry-based protein correlation profiling with published datasets, we assembled inventories of 1,666 mitochondrial proteins in T. brucei and 1,594 in L. tarentolae. These include 124 polypeptides not previously recognized as mitochondrial. Despite their phylogenetic distance, trypanosomes and leishmanias maintain highly conserved mitoproteomes, including about 700 components with no detectable homologs in other eukaryotes. Comparison of T. brucei insect and mammalian stages revealed similar mitoproteome compositions but globally reduced mitochondrial protein abundance in the latter, except for components of calcium homeostasis and the alternative oxidase pathway. We also detected ten kDNA-encoded proteins, including products of pan-edited transcripts. These inventories establish a framework for functional analysis of previously uncharacterized mitochondrial factors and illuminate innovations that have shaped kinetoplastid evolution.

abstract: The Microprocessor complex, minimally composed of DROSHA and DGCR8, is ubiquitously required for microRNA biogenesis. It also regulates the balance between pluripotency and differentiation through mRNA alternative splicing and mRNA cleavage. However, how these various activities are regulated remains incompletely understood. Both DROSHA and DGCR8 are phosphoproteins, and phosphorylation has been reported to influence their molecular functions. In this study, we identified residues in DGCR8 by mass spectrometry that were differentially phosphorylated in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) before and after differentiation into neuronal cells. This included S95 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in undifferentiated cells, and S238 that exhibited greater phosphorylation in differentiated cells. By means of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing of the endogenous Dgcr8 gene, we generated a homozygous S95A mESC clone and a heterozygous S238A/- mESC clone. Both mutants retained an mESC phenotype but exhibited altered Microprocessor-dependent functions and differentiation outcomes. When directed toward the neuronal lineage, the S238A/- mutant displayed elevated mRNA expression of neuronal progenitor markers even after 10 days, while both S95A and S238A/- mutants failed to generate cardiomyocytes in embryoid body differentiation cultures. Furthermore, MEK1/2 inhibition with a highly selective inhibitor partially phenocopied the transcriptional effects of S95A in mESCs, consistent with a potential contribution of ERK/MAPK signaling for S95 phosphorylation. Together, these findings support a role for site-specific DGCR8 phosphorylation in modulating Microprocessor-dependent processes and differentiation in mESCs, establishing DGCR8 phosphorylation as an important regulatory mechanism in the regulation of Microprocessor activity, especially for stem cell differentiation.

abstract: This is a Phase 1b/2 open-label study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and clinical effects of intravenous (IV) WVE-N531 in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). To participate in the study, patients must have a documented mutation of the DMD gene that is amenable to exon 53 skipping intervention. This study has 3 parts, Part A, Part B, including Part B Extension Arm, and Part C. Part A is completed. Part B is completed. Following completion of Part B, all patients elected to continue to receive study drug in the optional Part B open-label Extension Arm. Part C has been added to the study and will enroll new patients.
description:
Following completion of Part A, eligible patients rolled over into Part B to continue to receive treatment. In addition, new patients were enrolled up to a total of 11 patients in Part B. All patients received WVE-N531 at 10 mg/kg every other week (Q2W) until competent authority approval of a protocol update, when all patients were switched to Q4W dosing. Muscle biopsies were performed following 24 weeks and for new Part B patients (those that did not take part in Part A) following 48 weeks of treatment. Following completion of Part B, all patients elected to continue to receive study drug at Q4W for up to 1 year in an optional Part B Extension Arm.

In part C of the study, 13 new patients have been enrolled . All patients will undergo an open muscle biopsy, at baseline and following 24 weeks of treatment.

The primary endpoint for Part B is the measurement of dystrophin protein levels. Participants will also be evaluated for safety, tolerability, digital and functional endpoints.

The primary endpoint for Part C is the measurement of dystrophin protein levels. Participants will also be evaluated for safety, tolerability, digital and functional endpoints. Safety monitoring will occur through 10 months after the last dose.

abstract: The goal of the redePHine study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of ABO-101 in participants with primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). The trial will consist of 2 Study Periods. During the first Study Period, there will be 2 parts. In Part A, adult participants will be treated with a single ascending dose to identify a recommended dose. In Part B, pediatric participants will be treated with the recommended dose. Following the first Study Period, participants will start Study Period 2, a long-term monitoring program to comply with local and national requirements.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold immense therapeutic potential, yet their clinical translation is hindered by nonspecific cellular uptake and the complexity and cost of surface engineering. Here, we present the EZON (Easy OligoNucleotide) EV modification platform, a cost-effective, post-isolation modification system that addresses both limitations simultaneously. The EZON platform employs unmodified DNA aptamers that bind directly to tetraspanin proteins on EV surfaces, eliminating the need for cholesterol conjugation, covalent chemistry, or genetic engineering of producer cells. EVs are thus easily and rapidly functionalized in a single incubation step at substantially reduced oligonucleotide cost. The EZON platform enables dual functionality: (1) the oligonucleotide anchor (ONA) sequence inhibits nonspecific cellular uptake, while (2) the display strand enables targeted delivery through ligand-mediated internalization. We demonstrate that our optimized ONA construct efficiently functionalizes EVs from multiple mammalian cell types. Cancer cells selectively internalized EZON-modified EVs functionalized with AS1411, an aptamer that targets nucleolin, whereas off-target internalization was suppressed. The platform's versatility extends to protein display via histidine-tag aptamers and therapeutic cargo delivery, as demonstrated by targeted doxorubicin delivery to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells. This rapid, modular approach transforms unmodified EVs into precision delivery vehicles within hours, offering a scalable solution for targeted therapeutics.

abstract: Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as an effective experimental platform for bridging the long-standing gap between traditional in vitro cancer models and the biological complexity of actual tumors. These three-dimensional cultures (3D), derived directly from patient tissues, preserve essential architectural, genomic, and phenotypic characteristics of their tumors of origin, enabling more accurate modeling of tumor heterogeneity and disease evolution. Over the last decade, rapid methodological advances in organoid culture systems, extracellular matrices (ECMs), and growth factor optimization have facilitated the establishment of organoid models for a wide range of malignancies and the development of large living biobanks representing diverse patient populations. These models are increasingly being utilized to study cancer biology, elucidate mechanisms of treatment resistance, and evaluate patient-specific therapeutic responses, highlighting their potential as tools for precision oncology. However, important challenges remain, including incomplete representation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), variability in culture conditions, and limited scalability, and the need for greater standardization and validation. Consequently, although PDOs show considerable promise for translational research and personalized medicine, their routine clinical implementation remains largely investigational, and their clinical utility has not yet been fully established. This review examines the technological foundations of PDO generation, assesses their role as experimental models of tumor biology, and discusses their expanding applications in translational cancer research and precision oncology while highlighting key challenges that must be addressed before their widespread clinical adoption.

abstract: Mitochondria, as organelles with a critical role in maintaining cellular activities, are also vulnerable to dysfunction, which contributes substantially to the pathogenesis of various systemic diseases. Nanomaterials, owing to their tunable physicochemical properties and precise bio-interfacial capabilities, offer innovative platforms not only for delivering general mitochondria-targeted therapy but also for enabling-with promising potential-the emerging paradigms of mitochondrial transfer and transplantation. Nevertheless, a dedicated review systematically summarizing progress in this specific subfield is lacking. To fill this knowledge gap, this review provides a structured synthesis that spans from the biological basis of mitochondrial function and transfer to the broad applications of nanomaterials in mitochondria-targeted therapies, with a dedicated analysis of their roles in mitochondrial targeting, functional modulation, and gene editing. A key topic of this review is the emerging role of nanomaterials in assisting mitochondrial transplantation and transfer. By integrating these insights, this work bridges nanotechnology and mitochondrial medicine, offering a valuable resource for developing organelle-specific therapeutics.

abstract: Apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and ApoE4-directed gene editing and gene therapy have emerged as promising therapeutic strategies for AD, although they remain investigational and are not yet an established mainstream treatment. Interestingly, however, ApoE4 is reported to be associated with a reduced risk of retinal degenerative diseases such as glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and diabetic retinopathy (DR). Therefore, should ApoE4 gene editing therapy be approached with caution when AD occurs concurrently with glaucoma, AMD, or DR? In view of these and based on the existing literature, the present study detailed the distinct roles of ApoE4 in AD, glaucoma, AMD, and DR, with a purpose to offer valuable insights into subsequent ApoE4 gene editing therapies. We also summarise the ApoE-targeted therapeutic programmes currently in preclinical and early clinical development, delineate the remaining translational challenges, and discuss how patients with coexisting retinal neurodegenerative disease might be evaluated and monitored.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have reshaped modern vaccinology by enabling rapid antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and coordinated induction of humoral and cellular immunity. Their clinical success has established mRNA as a versatile platform for infectious diseases, cancer immunotherapy, and emerging therapeutic applications. However, expansion into cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and metabolic disorders imposes indication-specific requirements that cannot be addressed by uniform design strategies. Vaccine performance depends not only on antigen output, but also on how RNA architecture and delivery systems regulate innate sensing, intracellular trafficking, tissue distribution, and adaptive immune programming. In this review, we summarize bioengineering strategies for improving mRNA vaccine immunogenicity by coordinating antigen-expression efficiency with innate immune regulation. We compare non-replicating mRNA, self-amplifying RNA, and circular RNA in terms of expression kinetics, translational logic, safety considerations, and innate immune activation. We then discuss molecular engineering approaches that enhance stability, translation, and immune control, including optimization of cap structures, untranslated regions, poly(A) tails, nucleotide modifications, codon usage, and platform-specific designs for saRNA and circRNA. We further examine delivery systems, including lipid nanoparticles, exosomes, polymer-based carriers, virus-like particles, and hybrid platforms, emphasizing their dual roles in cargo transport and immune modulation. Finally, we discuss indication-specific design principles, manufacturing constraints, and translational challenges. We propose that next-generation mRNA vaccines will require disease-matched co-design of RNA molecules and delivery platforms to enhance antigen expression, tune immune activation, and strengthen clinical translation.

abstract: Diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2), a key enzyme in hepatic triglyceride (TG) synthesis, is considered a promising therapeutic target for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting conserved regions of human and mouse DGAT2 mRNA were designed, synthesized, and screened in vitro, leading to the identification of a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA, VX093L, which mediates potent DGAT2 mRNA knockdown in both human and mouse hepatocytes and exhibits sustained hepatic DGAT2 silencing in healthy mice. In a high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MASH mouse model, the effects of VX093L (1 or 3 mg/kg, biweekly) were evaluated in comparison with the approved drug resmetirom (10 mg/kg, daily). Eight-week treatment with VX093L potently silenced hepatic DGAT2 (>80%, p < 0.0001), thereby inhibiting hepatic TG synthesis, resulting in significantly ameliorating hepatic steatosis. Notably, the improvement in steatosis translated into effective attenuation of fibrosis, with 1 mg/kg VX093L exhibiting better anti-fibrotic efficacy compared to resmetirom, and this benefit was not accompanied by increased inflammation. In conclusion, VX093L represents a promising siRNA-based therapeutic for the treatment of MASH.

title: Liver-Targeted DGAT2 siRNA Ameliorates Steatosis and Fibrosis in a High-Fat Diet-Induced MASH Mouse Model.

abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification

abstract: Reliable assessment of disease status and therapeutic response in osteosarcoma remains an unmet clinical need. Integrative bioinformatics analysis and protein-level verification in paired clinical specimens prioritized secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, osteopontin) as a liquid biopsy target associated with osteosarcoma progression and patient survival. On this basis, CRUMP, a CRISPR-Cas12a and FUSE Probe-based dual-mode biosensing platform, was developed for SPP1 quantification. A bifunctional NH2-ZIF-8 probe co-immobilizes the components required for target recognition and Cas12a activation, while MoS2@AuNPs interfaces transduce the resulting signals. Signal amplification is achieved through a unipoint-anchored multisite cascade based on a DNA tetrahedron-HCR architecture, enabling one-to-multiple parallel amplification while balancing stability and sensitivity. A single Cas12a cleavage event simultaneously decreases the electrochemical (EC) signal and increases the fluorescence (FL) signal. These reciprocal changes allow the two readouts to provide an internal consistency check for each measurement. Each channel covers more than five orders of magnitude, with detection limits of 167.7 fg/mL for EC and 331.6 fg/mL for FL. The broad measurement ranges allow most serum samples to be analyzed directly, without the per-sample dilution optimization that ELISA requires, and the complete analysis takes only approximately 85 min. Validation across osteosarcoma cell lines, clinical specimens, and tumor-bearing mouse models provided preliminary evidence for the feasibility of CRUMP in SPP1 quantification and endpoint assessment of chemotherapeutic response. By combining biomarker prioritization, biosensor engineering, and preliminary application testing, this work presents CRUMP as a candidate platform for SPP1-based assessment of osteosarcoma and its therapeutic response.

title: Unipoint-anchored cascade amplification strategy integrating FUSE probe-activated CRISPR-Cas12a for dual mode osteopontin detection toward osteosarcoma assessment and therapeutic response evaluation.

abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

abstract: Degenerative diseases continue to impose a substantial global health burden with limited curative options. Neurodegenerative diseases, the principal focus of this review, are among the largest contributors to this burden. Stem cell therapies have emerged as a promising approach, offering the potential to replace lost cells, modulate pathological microenvironments, and restore tissue function through both direct cell replacement and paracrine mechanisms. However, conventional stem cell strategies encounter persistent obstacles including immune rejection, tumorigenicity, poor engraftment, and limited long-term efficacy in chronic disease settings. This narrative review synthesizes recent and emerging innovations in stem cell therapy for neurodegenerative diseases across four major domains: (i) emerging mechanisms of stem cell action, including activation of dormant neural stem cells (NSCs), exosome-based cell-free therapies, and rejuvenation of aged stem cells; (ii) emerging cell types such as pre-morula stem cells (PMSCs), perinatal stem cells, SSEA-4+ human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs), and iPSC-derived mesenchymal progenitor cells (MiMPCs); (iii) advanced delivery platforms including three-dimensional (3D) biomaterial scaffolds, injectable hydrogels, and stem cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CMNPs); and (iv) gene-editing strategies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9-mediated generation of hypoimmunogenic induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines for allogeneic, off-the-shelf cell therapies. Key translational gaps, including standardization of exosome isolation and scaffold fabrication protocols, long-term safety and immunogenicity assessment, and ethical and regulatory frameworks, are critically evaluated, and future research directions are proposed. In addition, the review states the level of evidence (in vitro, animal, or human) supporting each approach and summarizes their clinical status in a single table. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to realizing the full potential of stem cell-based regenerative medicine for degenerative diseases.

abstract: Reactive oxygen species generate a family of oxidized guanine species that serve as important biomarkers of oxidative damage. Here, we report the development of a fluorogenic RNA switch that selectively recognizes oxidized guanine species. We first systematically characterized an oxidized guanine RNA aptamer, defining its minimum functional binding domain and molecular recognition profile. Structural minimization produced a compact aptamer with higher affinity than the full-length sequence that retained broad recognition of structurally diverse oxidized guanine species while discriminating against their unmodified counterparts. We subsequently incorporated the optimized aptamer into fluorogenic RNA switch architectures, revealing that fluorescence activation required iterative optimization of aptamer topology, scaffold architecture, and communication-linker design. The resulting fluorogenic RNA switch exhibited target-dependent fluorescence activation while retaining the aptamer's molecular recognition profile. This work establishes a fluorogenic RNA switch for oxidized guanine species and highlights the importance of systematic aptamer characterization and optimization in fluorogenic RNA switch development.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human, animal, agricultural, and environmental health, driven by horizontal and vertical gene transfer. Conventional wastewater treatment removes 63-94% of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) but fails to eliminate ARGs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria, while generating toxic sludge. This review evaluates advanced biomaterials, including silver and gold nanoparticles, reactive oxygen species, magnetic nanocomposites, targeted disruption of metabolic pathways, carbon-based sorbents, biopolymers, metal-organic frameworks, functionalized enzymes/peptides, and engineered biofilms, for reducing ARG and resistant-bacteria loads, inhibiting horizontal gene transfer, and reducing the selective pressure exerted by residual antibiotics. These approaches offer enhanced performance across wastewater/agriculture/air/food supply chain systems. Challenges in scalability, ecological safety, and regulation remain, requiring integration with AI monitoring, CRISPR tools, and One Health strategies. This review aims to summarize and discuss the literature on the development and use of innovative biomaterial-based intervention strategies that address the environmental aspects of AMR in order to provide a comprehensive overview of what has been learned and developed to date.

abstract: Epigenetic regulation and gene transcription are dynamically modulated by extracellular signals, including focal adhesions; however, the role of integrins in these processes remains poorly understood. In this study in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, (HNSCC), we combined investigations in physiological three-dimensional, matrix-embedded cell models and patient-derived organoids with multi-omics analyses, bioinformatics and artificial intelligence, to unmask the integrin effector signaling network that reshapes chromatin to drive cancer. Among the 12 α/β1 integrin receptors, α7 integrin (ITGA7) emerged as the most potent modulator of histone post-translational modifications, associated with significant changes in gene transcription and chromatin accessibility. Depletion of ITGA7, achieved independently by CRISPR/Cas9 knockout and RNA interference, reduced chromatin accessibility at the AURKA locus and downregulated an AURKA-centered transcriptional program. Mechanistically, phosphoproteomics revealed significant inhibition of MAPK- and PI3K/AKT-dependent signaling with concomitant functional impairment of cell cycling and cell survival upon ITGA7 depletion. Across all analyses, machine-learning-based feature selection consistently nominated AURKA as the dominant downstream node, and tumor ITGA7 expression stratified patient overall survival in a non-linear manner. In summary, these findings establish α7 integrin as a key co-regulator of chromatin accessibility and gene transcription in HPV-negative HNSCC, acting through an AURKA-centered axis that couples adhesion signaling to cell cycle control and patient survival, and nominate AURKA, potentially targetable with clinical Aurora-A inhibitors such as alisertib, as an actionable therapeutic node downstream of the currently non-druggable ITGA7.

abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.
